summary: Phaxsi is a free, offline-capable web tool that helps planners, educators and the public compare candidate landing sites and dates near the lunar south pole. For each location and date it shows, from real NASA LOLA terrain and hourly 2027 ephemerides, how long the Sun and the Earth are both above the local horizon (energy and direct-to-Earth line of sight), how long the longest interruption lasts, and what the terrain looks like (slope, relief, roughness). It gives a transparent recommendation, a Plan B, and a side-by-side A/B comparison. It matters because choosing where and when to land near the pole depends on a few hours of light and communication, and this makes that trade-off visible and easy to explain.
details:
What it does: phaxsi is an interactive map and analysis tool for the lunar south pole (90°S to 80°S). The user sets mission dates (arrival, launch or none) and a surface-operation length, then selects locations. For each one, phaxsi computes the share of time the Sun (upper limb) and the Earth (centre) are above the local LOLA horizon, the share when both are visible, and the longest interruption. It ranks candidates with a transparent rule (user constraints, then simultaneous visibility within a 1-percentage-point evidence margin, then shortest interruption, then slope, then roughness), proposes a Plan B (alternative site or date), and compares any two locations A/B. An optional energy estimate uses only hardware values entered by the user.

How it works: hourly Sun and Earth visibility for 2027 (8,761 instants) was precomputed in Python from a JPL Horizons ephemeris and local horizon masks built from LOLA terrain, then exported as static data. The app runs entirely in the browser (HTML, CSS, vanilla JavaScript, canvas) and also works offline by opening index.html. Terrain layers (hillshade, slope, elevation, uncertainty, LOLA counts, permanent shadow) are PNGs derived from LOLA GeoTIFFs without resampling or invented detail.

Coverage (stated honestly): 15 x 15 grids at 1 km cover 6 regions (Haworth, Malapert Massif, Nobile Rim 1, Nobile Rim 2, de Gerlache Rim 2 and Peak Near Shackleton), 1,350 nodes in total. For four regions of the NASA 2024 list without published boundaries (Peak near Cabeus B, Mons Mouton, Mons Mouton Plateau, Slater Plain) we analyse only the 37 representative candidate sites of Wueller et al. (2026), as individual points, with no regional heatmap. Candidate sites are not certified landing sites.

Limits: geometric visibility, not a communications link budget; 2027 only; terrain slope does not establish bearing capacity; no temperature (no Diviner data) and no LROC imagery.

Tools: Python (data precomputation and verification), HTML/CSS/JavaScript, HTML canvas, headless-browser regression tests (about 30,000 automated checks), static hosting on Vercel.

Source code: https://github.com/vuhn204/phaxsi
dataRefs: LOLA south-polar products (DEM, hillshade, errors, observation counts, effective resolution, permanent shadow), NASA GSFC PGDA, Barker et al. 2023
NASA candidate Artemis III landing regions (2024 list), region names and coordinates from PGDA
LRO LOLA polar GDR (2017 preliminary, LRO-L-LOLA-4-GDR-V1.0), used for local horizon masks
JPL Horizons ephemeris (Sun, Earth, Moon geometry; downloaded once on 2026-11-14)
projectRefs: Wueller et al. (2026), J. Geophys. Res. Planets 131, e2025JE009434 (37 candidate sites)
Wueller et al. (2026) supplementary dataset, Landing_Sites.zip, Zenodo (CC-BY-4.0)
